message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a C++ URL parser library **purely as a black box**.

The only artifact is the compiled binary: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable
There is NO library source available anywhere on disk (do not go looking for url_parser.h/.cpp — it does not exist). Do not try to disassemble or run 'strings'. Use ONLY behavioral probing: run the binary with argument values and observe stdout.

Usage: /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "<url>"
With fewer than 2 argv entries it returns exit code 1 and prints nothing.

It prints EXACTLY 18 lines, in this order (one per line, via std::cout << x << std::endl):
 1  scheme()          (string)
 2  authority()       (string)
 3  userinfo()        (string)
 4  host()            (string)
 5  port()            (int, prints -1 when absent)
 6  path()            (string)
 7  query()           (string)
 8  fragment()        (string)
 9  has_scheme()      (bool printed as 1/0)
10  has_authority()
11  has_userinfo()
12  has_host()
13  has_port()
14  has_path()
15  has_query()
16  has_fragment()
17  to_string()       (string)
18  is_valid()        (bool 1/0)

A labeled probe helper already exists at /tmp/probe.sh (takes any number of url args). If missing, recreate it:

  cat > /tmp/probe.sh << 'EOS'
  #!/bin/bash
  LABELS=(scheme authority userinfo host port path query fragment has_scheme has_authority has_userinfo has_host has_port has_path has_query has_fragment to_string is_valid)
  for arg in "$@"; do
    echo "=== INPUT: [$arg]"
    mapfile -t out < <(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$arg"; echo "EXIT:$?")
    for i in "${!LABELS[@]}"; do printf "  %-14s [%s]\n" "${LABELS[$i]}" "${out[$i]}"; done
  done
  EOS
  chmod +x /tmp/probe.sh

Note: /tmp/probe.sh renders empty fields as []. For inputs containing characters bash would mangle, invoke the binary directly with careful quoting, or use printf/hexdump to inspect raw bytes:
  /workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$URL" | od -c | head -40

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verified; you may re-verify but do not spend most of your budget here):
- A scheme is recognized ONLY when the literal "://" appears. "mailto:user@example.com" yields NO scheme and the entire input becomes path. "//example.com/path" yields no scheme and the whole thing is path (authority is parsed only when "://" was found).
- scheme() is LOWERCASED ("HTTP://EXAMPLE.COM" -> scheme "http"), but host() case is preserved ("EXAMPLE.COM").
- authority() is RECONSTRUCTED from userinfo/host/port, not the raw substring: "http://example.com:80abc" -> authority "example.com:80"; "http://example.com:" -> authority "example.com".
- port parsing behaves like std::stoi + a range check: "80abc"->80, "+80"->80, " 80"->80, "065"->65, "0"->0, but "-80"->absent, "65536"->absent, "2147483648"->absent, "abc"->absent, ""->absent. Absent port prints -1 with has_port 0 and is omitted from authority()/to_string().
- Splitting after authority: the FIRST '#' splits off fragment (so "#a#b" -> fragment "a#b"); then within the part BEFORE that '#', the FIRST '?' splits off query. "/p#a?b" -> fragment "a?b", no query.
- has_*() appear to be "field is non-empty" for strings ("http://example.com/#" -> fragment "" and has_fragment 0), and has_port() is port != -1. BUT has_authority() is NOT simply "authority string non-empty": "http://:8080" gives authority ":8080" yet has_authority 0 (host is empty there) — pin down the real rule.
- No path normalization ("/a/./b/../c" preserved), no percent-decoding ("%7E" preserved).
- is_valid(): "" -> 0, "http://" -> 0, "http://:8080" -> 0, but "example.com" -> 1, "/just/a/path" -> 1, "mailto:user@example.com" -> 1.

YOUR JOB: exhaustively probe your assigned family below. Run MANY probes (dozens — at least 40 distinct inputs; more is better). For every behavior you claim, you MUST have run the exact input. Derive precise, implementable rules (as if writing pseudocode), and explicitly flag anything ambiguous or surprising.

Return findings as structured output. Rules must be stated so a programmer can implement them without further probing. Include the concrete probe evidence (input -> the specific field values that matter) for each rule. Prefer many small precise rules over few vague ones.

YOUR ASSIGNED FAMILY:
PORT NUMERIC PARSING — exhaustive std::stoi-vs-something-else determination.
Establish the exact numeric parse and the exact accept/reject predicate. Probe (all as "http://h:<X>"): "0", "1", "80", "65535", "65536", "65537", "70000", "99999", "-1", "-0", "+0", "+65535", "007", "0x10", "0b1", "1e3", "1.5", "80.9", " 80", "\t80", "80 ", "80abc", "abc80", "8a0", "2147483647", "2147483648", "4294967296", "18446744073709551617", "99999999999999999999", "", ":", "+", "-", " ", "٣" (Arabic-Indic digit), "１２３" (fullwidth digits), "80%20". Determine: (a) does it skip leading whitespace, (b) does it accept a leading +/-, (c) does it stop at the first non-digit (stoi) or require the whole string to be digits, (d) what is the exact accepted numeric range (is it 0..65535? 1..65535? 0..65535 inclusive?), (e) does an out-of-range or unparsable port cause the ':'+text to be dropped entirely from host (host stays clean) — and does it ever end up appended to host or path instead? (f) Does a rejected port affect is_valid()? Also probe a rejected port combined with a path: "http://h:abc/p?q#f" — confirm path/query/fragment still parse. State the final predicate as exact pseudocode.

#!/bin/bash
# Labeled probe: prints each field with a label
LABELS=(scheme authority userinfo host port path query fragment has_scheme has_authority has_userinfo has_host has_port has_path has_query has_fragment to_string is_valid)
for arg in "$@"; do
  echo "=== INPUT: [$arg]"
  mapfile -t out < <(/workspace/dataset/test18_executable "$arg"; echo "EXIT:$?")
  n=${#out[@]}
  if [ "${out[$((n-1))]}" != "EXIT:0" ]; then
    echo "  NONZERO/ABNORMAL: last=${out[$((n-1))]} lines=$n"
  fi
  for i in "${!LABELS[@]}"; do
    printf "  %-14s [%s]\n" "${LABELS[$i]}" "${out[$i]}"
  done
  echo "  (total lines incl exit marker: $n)"
done

input.family: PORT NUMERIC PARSING (host:port split + std::stoi-style parse + range predicate)

rules.rule: Port text extraction: after the authority has been isolated (authority = text after "://" up to the first '/', '?' or '#'), and after userinfo is split off at '@', the remaining host_part is split at the FIRST ':' . host = text before it, port_text = ENTIRE remainder after it (may itself contain ':', '@' is impossible here since userinfo split already happened). Evidence: "http://h:12:34:56" -> host "h", port 12; "http://h:80:90" -> host "h", port 80; "http://h::" -> host "h", port absent (port_text ":" is unparsable). Not the last ':': last-colon splitting would have given host "h:12:34" / "h:".

Numeric parse is exactly std::stoi(port_text) wrapped in try/catch (base 10, no endptr check): (1) skip leading C-locale whitespace, (2) accept one optional '+' or '-', (3) consume the maximal run of ASCII digits, (4) STOP at the first non-digit and IGNORE the rest (no requirement that the whole string be digits). Evidence: "80abc"->80, "8a0"->8, "80 "->80, "6553 5"->6553, "0x10"->0, "0b1"->0, "1e3"->1, "6e4"->6, "1.5"->1, "80.9"->80, "6553.6"->6553, "1,000"->1, "65,536"->65, "65535abc"->65535, "80%20"->80, "80٣"->80, "80:"->80.

Leading whitespace IS skipped, and it is C-locale isspace: space, tab, newline, vertical tab, form feed, carriage return all work, and multiple/mixed whitespace works. Evidence: "http://h: 80"->80, "http://h:\t80"->80, "http://h:\n80"->80, "http://h:\v80"->80, "http://h:\f80"->80, "http://h:\r80"->80, "http://h:  80"->80, "http://h: \t\n 80"->80. U+00A0 NBSP (bytes C2 A0) is NOT whitespace: "http://h:\xc2\xa080" -> port absent.

A single leading sign is accepted; whitespace may precede the sign but NOT follow it, and only one sign is allowed. Evidence: "+80"->80, "+00080"->80, "+65535"->65535, " +80"->80; but "+ 80"->absent, "- 80"->absent, " -80"->absent(negative), "++80"->absent, "--80"->absent, "+-80"->absent, bare "+"->absent, bare "-"->absent.

Accept/reject predicate on the parsed value: accept iff 0 <= value <= 65535 inclusive (65535 is valid, 0 is valid, so the range is 0..65535, NOT 1..65535). Evidence: "0"->0 accepted (has_port 1, to_string "http://h:0"), "1"->1, "65534"->65534, "65535"->65535 accepted; "65536","65537","70000","99999","655350","65535000","65536abc","2147483646" -> all absent.

Negative parsed values are rejected, but the sign is applied BEFORE the range check, so "-0" is accepted as 0. Evidence: "http://h:-0" -> port 0, has_port 1, authority "h:0", to_string "http://h:0"; "http://h:-1", "http://h:-80", "http://h:-65535", "http://h:-2147483648", "http://h:-2147483649" -> all port -1 / has_port 0.

Unparsable (zero digits consumed) => absent. This covers empty, whitespace-only, sign-only, and any string whose first non-space/non-sign char is not an ASCII digit. Evidence: "http://h:"->absent, "http://h::"->absent, "http://h: "->absent, "http://h:abc"->absent, "http://h:abc80"->absent, "http://h:abc:80"->absent, "http://h:.80"->absent, "http://h:_80"->absent, "http://h:%2080"->absent.

Only ASCII '0'-'9' count as digits — non-ASCII digit forms are rejected (no Unicode digit handling, no locale digit handling). Evidence: "http://h:٣" (U+0663 Arabic-Indic three) -> absent; "http://h:٣80" -> absent (stops immediately); "http://h:１２３" (fullwidth) -> absent; but "http://h:80٣" -> 80 (ASCII digits first, trailing garbage ignored).

Overflow beyond int range behaves as std::stoi's out_of_range => absent (indistinguishable from, and equivalent to, the >65535 rejection). Evidence: "2147483647"->absent, "2147483648"->absent, "4294967296"->absent, "18446744073709551617"->absent, "99999999999999999999"->absent, "21474836470"->absent, "80000000000000000000000"->absent, 1000 '9' chars -> absent. Implementation note: you can implement this as a single check 0<=value<=65535 using arbitrary/64-bit precision — any value that would overflow int also exceeds 65535, so the observable behavior is identical.

Leading zeros are decimal, not octal, and do not cause overflow no matter how many there are. Evidence: "007"->7, "065"->65, "0080"->80, "00"->0, "0000"->0, "0777"->777 (not 511), "000000000000065535"->65535, "000000000000065536"->absent, 1000 zeros followed by "80"->80, 1000 zeros alone ->0, "000000000002147483648"->absent.

On rejection the ':' and the entire port text are DROPPED ENTIRELY: host keeps only the text before the ':', and the rejected text never appears in host(), path(), query(), fragment(), authority(), or to_string(). Evidence: "http://h:abc" -> host "h", path "", authority "h", to_string "http://h"; "http://h:65536" -> authority "h", to_string "http://h"; "http://h:80000000000000000000000" -> to_string "http://h".

A rejected/absent port has NO effect on is_valid(): is_valid stays 1 as long as the rest of the URL is valid. Evidence: "http://h:abc" -> is_valid 1; "http://h:65536" -> 1; "http://h:" -> 1; "http://h:-1" -> 1; "http://h:2147483648/p?q#f" -> 1. Conversely a VALID port does not rescue an empty host: "http://:80" -> port 80, has_port 1, authority ":80", to_string "http://:80", is_valid 0.

Path/query/fragment parsing is unaffected by port rejection — the authority terminator scan happens before port parsing. Evidence: "http://h:abc/p?q#f" -> host "h", port -1, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", to_string "http://h/p?q#f"; "http://h:65536/p?q#f" -> same shape; "http://h:2147483648/p?q#f" -> same; "http://h:80abc/p?q#f" -> port 80, path "/p", query "q", fragment "f", to_string "http://h:80/p?q#f".

The port text never extends past the authority terminator, so '/', '?' and '#' effectively terminate the port digits (in addition to stoi stopping there anyway). Evidence: "http://h:8?0" -> port 8, query "0" (NOT port 80); "http://h:8#0" -> port 8, fragment "0"; "http://h:80?q=1" -> port 80 + query "q=1"; "http://h:80#f" -> port 80 + fragment "f"; "http://h:80/" -> port 80, path "/"; "http://h:0/" -> port 0, path "/".

A ':' that appears after the authority ends is never a port: it is ordinary path/query/fragment text. Evidence: "http://h/x:80" -> port -1, path "/x:80"; "http://h?x:80" -> query "x:80"; "http://h#x:80" -> fragment "x:80". And with no "://" there is no port at all: "example.com:8080" -> path "example.com:8080", port -1; "//h:8080" -> path "//h:8080", port -1.

Userinfo is split off BEFORE the host:port split, so a ':' inside userinfo is not a port and a ':' after '@' is. Evidence: "http://u:p@h:80" -> userinfo "u:p", host "h", port 80; "http://u:80@h" -> userinfo "u:80", host "h", port -1; "http://h:80@x" -> userinfo "h:80", host "x", port -1; "http://@h:80" -> userinfo "", host "h", port 80, authority "h:80"; "http://u:p@h:65536/x" -> userinfo "u:p", host "h", port -1, path "/x", to_string "http://u:p@h/x".

There is NO IPv6 bracket handling: the first ':' inside '[...]' is treated as the port delimiter, mangling the host. Evidence: "http://[::1]:8080" -> host "[", port -1 (port_text ":1]:8080" is unparsable), authority "[", to_string "http://[", is_valid 1.

No default-port suppression and no scheme-specific port logic: an accepted port is always echoed in authority() and to_string(), including 0 and scheme-default ports. Evidence: "http://h:80" -> to_string "http://h:80"; "https://h:443" -> "https://h:443"; "ftp://h:21" -> "ftp://h:21"; "http://h:0" -> "http://h:0". Port is printed canonically (re-serialized from the int), so leading zeros/sign/whitespace/trailing junk are normalized away: "http://h:+00080" -> to_string "http://h:80".

has_port() == (port() != -1), equivalently (port() >= 0). Since -1 can never be produced by a successful parse (negatives are rejected), the two formulations are behaviorally identical. Absent port prints exactly "-1" on line 5 with has_port 0.

Exact pseudocode for the predicate:
  parse_port(port_text) -> optional<int>:
    i = 0
    while i < len && isspace_c(port_text[i]): i++          // " \t\n\v\f\r"
    neg = false
    if i < len and (port_text[i]=='+' or port_text[i]=='-'):
        neg = (port_text[i]=='-'); i++
    start = i
    while i < len and '0' <= port_text[i] <= '9': i++
    if i == start: return NONE                              // stoi -> invalid_argument
    mag = decimal_value(port_text[start..i))                 // arbitrary precision
    if mag > 2147483647: return NONE                         // stoi -> out_of_range
    v = neg ? -mag : mag
    if v < 0 or v > 65535: return NONE                       // range check
    return v
  // NONE => port = -1, has_port = false, ':'+text omitted from authority() and to_string(); is_valid() unaffected.

ambiguities: std::stoi vs std::stol/stoll/strtol is behaviorally indistinguishable here: every value that would overflow int (>2147483647) also exceeds 65535, so both paths yield 'absent'. Likewise std::stoul cannot be ruled out: stoul("-0")==0 (accepted, matches) and stoul("-80") wraps to a huge value (>65535, rejected, also matches). Implementing as 'optional ws, optional sign, digits, accept iff 0<=signed value<=65535' reproduces all observed outputs.

Whether the range test is written as (v < 0 || v > 65535) or (v >= 0 && v <= 65535) or against an unsigned 16-bit cap is unobservable; 65535 accepted / 65536 rejected is the only boundary evidence and it is unambiguous.
has_port() could be implemented as port != -1 or port >= 0; since a successful parse can never produce a negative value, the two are indistinguishable.

isspace() is locale-dependent in principle. All six C-locale whitespace bytes are skipped; NBSP (C2 A0) is not. I could not test under a non-C locale, so a locale-sensitive difference cannot be fully excluded (the binary presumably never calls setlocale, so the classic 'C' locale set is the safe implementation).
A literal NUL byte inside the port text could not be tested (bash strips it from argv), so behavior of an embedded '\0' is unknown — likely unreachable via argv anyway.

SURPRISING (worth a regression test): "http://h:-0" yields port 0 with has_port 1, i.e. a negative-signed input is accepted. Also surprising: "http://h:8?0" -> port 8 (not 80) because the authority terminator is found before the numeric parse.
SURPRISING: a rejected port silently deletes the ':'+text, so to_string() is lossy and NOT round-trip stable for inputs like "http://h:abc" -> "http://h" and "http://h:65536" -> "http://h".
